idea: Translate “at most” as ≤ and “at least” as ≥, solve like an equation, then decide which whole numbers the context allows. Round in the direction the inequality forces, not to the nearest whole number.
trap: Rounding 13.6 up to 14 when the limit says “at most.”
desmos: Graphing the inequality shows the boundary, but the whole-number decision at the end is yours.

items.stem: A club has $167 to spend on a party. The room costs $31, and each guest's meal costs $6. What is the greatest number of guests the club can feed without spending more than $167?
items.explain: 31+6g≤167 gives g≤6136​≈22.67. The number of guests is a whole number, so the greatest is 22; rounding up would go over budget.

items.stem: A van can carry at most 1049 kilograms. It carries a driver who weighs 73 kilograms, small boxes that weigh 22.5 kilograms each, and large boxes that weigh 40 kilograms each. If it carries exactly 3 times as many small boxes as large boxes, what is the greatest number of large boxes it can carry?
items.explain: With L large boxes there are 3L small ones: 73+22.5(3L)+40L≤1049, so 107.5L≤976 and L≤9.08. The greatest whole number is 9.

items.stem: Mira earns $15 per hour tutoring and $11 per hour at a café. This week she wants to earn at least $391 while working at most 28 hours in total. If she works only whole numbers of hours, what is the least number of hours she can spend tutoring?
items.explain: To tutor as little as possible, fill the rest of the 28 hours at the café. With t hours tutoring: 15t+11(28−t)≥391, so 4t≥83 and t≥20.75. The least whole number is 21.
